explanations.answer: His brothers and all his sons
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Jeremiah the prophet takes Jaazaniah, his brothers and all his sons, "…the entire house of the Rechabites…" (Jeremiah 35:3). The text says the ENTIRE house, so nobody gets to sit this one out. That's a lot of folks to walk into one room.

Close to the room, but not the guest list. The officials' chamber is only a landmark here, because the room sits near it (Jeremiah 35:4). The ones Jeremiah brings are Jaazaniah, his brothers and all his sons. The officials just happen to be neighbors.

I can see why you'd think so, since Jeremiah brings them into the house of the LORD. But the text names Jaazaniah, his brothers and all his sons, the entire house of the Rechabites (Jeremiah 35:3). Priests and Levites aren't named there. Right building, but that's not who the verse lists.

explanations.answer: He told them never to drink it
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. They say Jonadab commanded, "Neither you nor your descendants are ever to drink wine." (Jeremiah 35:6). Never means never, and there's no loophole in that sentence. I've looked for loopholes in my own rules for years, and I respect this.

explanations.answer: He told them to drink only at feasts
explanations.explanation: Nice try, but a feast clause isn't in there. The Rechabites quote Jonadab: "Neither you nor your descendants are ever to drink wine." (Jeremiah 35:6). No exceptions listed, not even a big party. That's a short rule with no fine print.

explanations.answer: He told them to drink only at home
explanations.explanation: Home is a natural guess, since in a minute we learn they live in tents (Jeremiah 35:7). Jonadab's command was, "Neither you nor your descendants are ever to drink wine." (Jeremiah 35:6). No at-home exception. Not at home, not anywhere.

Tents it is, baker. Jonadab said, "…you must live in tents all your lives…" (Jeremiah 35:7). All their lives, not just a camping weekend. I get nervous when my oven mitt goes missing, so I can't imagine a whole life with no walls.

Caves are a fair guess for people with no house, but that's not what the text says. Jonadab told them, "…you must live in tents all your lives…" (Jeremiah 35:7). Tents. The Rechabites repeat it later when they say, "…we have lived in tents…" (Jeremiah 35:10).
Towns is a fair guess, but that's not the word. Jonadab said they were never to build a house, and then, "…you must live in tents all your lives…" (Jeremiah 35:7). So the blank is tents.

explanations.answer: So they could live a long time in the land
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. Jonadab says to live in tents "…so that you may live a long time in the land where you wander." (Jeremiah 35:7). That's the reason the text gives, so I'll stick to it. Sometimes a rule comes with its reason attached, and that's a kindness.

explanations.answer: So they could always be ready for war
explanations.explanation: War is a reasonable thing to think of with tents, but the text doesn't say that. The reason Jonadab gave was "…so that you may live a long time in the land where you wander." (Jeremiah 35:7). I won't make up reasons for him. Long life in the land, that's it.

explanations.answer: So they could stay far away from kings
explanations.explanation: That's a creative one, but kings aren't mentioned in Jonadab's reason. He said to live in tents "…so that you may live a long time in the land where you wander." (Jeremiah 35:7). The reason is a long life in the land. I'm not going to guess past that.

True, baker. The Rechabites say, "…we have not drunk wine all our lives—neither we nor our wives nor our sons and daughters." (Jeremiah 35:8). The whole family, all their lives. That's a whole household keeping one rule.

Not false, baker. The Rechabites say, "…we have not drunk wine all our lives—neither we nor our wives nor our sons and daughters." (Jeremiah 35:8). So wives, sons and daughters are all included. Nobody in the family is the exception.

explanations.answer: To escape the armies coming in
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. They said, "Come, let us go into Jerusalem to escape the armies of the Chaldeans and the Arameans." (Jeremiah 35:11). So the Rechabites went into Jerusalem to escape the armies. That's the reason they gave.

explanations.answer: To join the army of Judah
explanations.explanation: Fighting is a bold thought, but the text gives a different reason. The Rechabites said, "Come, let us go into Jerusalem to escape the armies of the Chaldeans and the Arameans." (Jeremiah 35:11). They went to escape, not to enlist. Nothing here says they joined any army.

explanations.answer: To buy land and finally settle
explanations.explanation: Settling down doesn't match what they say. Jonadab told them not to build a house or sow seed or plant a vineyard, and they say, "…we have lived in tents…" (Jeremiah 35:7, 10). The reason they came was, "…to escape the armies of the Chaldeans and the Arameans." (Jeremiah 35:11). They stayed in Jerusalem, but nothing here says they settled.

Right, baker. God says, "The words of Jonadab son of Rechab have been carried out." (Jeremiah 35:14). He holds up the Rechabites as people who did what they were told. I think that's the kind of compliment you remember.

explanations.answer: They were too hard to keep
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that, baker. God says, "The words of Jonadab son of Rechab have been carried out." (Jeremiah 35:14). He adds that Jonadab's sons have not drunk wine to this very day. Carried out is the word, not too hard.

Forgotten would be the opposite of what God says. He says, "The words of Jonadab son of Rechab have been carried out." (Jeremiah 35:14). He adds that the sons have not drunk wine to this very day because they obeyed their forefather's command. Carried out, baker, not forgotten.
Not quite, baker. God says, "…I have spoken to you again and again, and you have not obeyed Me!" (Jeremiah 35:14). Again and again is the opposite of only once. So the answer is False.
False is right, baker. God says, "…I have spoken to you again and again, and you have not obeyed Me!" (Jeremiah 35:14). So He spoke many times, not once. The problem wasn't a lack of words.

Yes, baker. The prophets proclaimed, "Turn now, each of you, from your wicked ways, and correct your actions." (Jeremiah 35:15). God says He sent them again and again. And of the people He says, "…you have not inclined your ear or listened to Me."

Nope, no building project in this message. The prophets proclaimed, "Turn now, each of you, from your wicked ways, and correct your actions." (Jeremiah 35:15). It was about turning and correcting their actions. Nothing about construction.

That's backward, baker. The prophets said, "Live in the land that I have given to you and your fathers." (Jeremiah 35:15). Their message to turn from wicked ways came with an invitation to stay. Nobody was telling them to pack up.

Gods, baker, GODS! The prophets said, "Do not go after other gods to serve them." (Jeremiah 35:15). Notice the two actions in that warning: going after them and serving them. It comes in the same message as turning from wicked ways.
Kings is a fair guess, but the text says something else. The prophets said, "Do not go after other gods to serve them." (Jeremiah 35:15). The word is gods, and the warning is about serving them.

Nations is a decent guess, but the text says something else. The prophets said, "Do not go after other gods to serve them." (Jeremiah 35:15). The warning was about other gods. That's the word that fills the blank.

Disaster, baker. God says, "…I will bring to Judah and to all the residents of Jerusalem all the disaster I have pronounced against them…" (Jeremiah 35:17). It's a heavy line. He gives the reason too: "…I have spoken to them but they have not obeyed, and I have called to them but they have not answered."

I wish that were the word, baker, but it's a heavy one. God says, "…I will bring to Judah and to all the residents of Jerusalem all the disaster I have pronounced against them…" (Jeremiah 35:17). The blessing in this passage goes to the Rechabites (Jeremiah 35:19). This part is hard to read.

I wish it were peace, baker, but this part is heavy. God says, "…I will bring to Judah and to all the residents of Jerusalem all the disaster I have pronounced against them…" (Jeremiah 35:17). The word is disaster. He says it comes because they did not obey or answer.

explanations.answer: A man to stand before God always
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The LORD of Hosts says, "Jonadab son of Rechab will never fail to have a man to stand before Me." (Jeremiah 35:19). Because they obeyed, that promise came to the family. I think that beats any trophy I could stamp.

explanations.answer: Fields and vineyards of their own
explanations.explanation: Fields and vineyards aren't the promise here. The Rechabites say they have not owned vineyards or fields or crops (Jeremiah 35:9). The promise God gives is, "Jonadab son of Rechab will never fail to have a man to stand before Me." (Jeremiah 35:19). It's about a man standing before God.

A throne would be a big promise, but it's not in the text. The LORD of Hosts says, "Jonadab son of Rechab will never fail to have a man to stand before Me." (Jeremiah 35:19). The promise is about a man standing before God. Ruling Jerusalem isn't mentioned.
